The Story of King Dhandatt

I bow to Lord Jina, worshipped by the gods and adorned with infinite knowledge and vision, and I write the sacred story of King Dhandatt.

In the land of Andh, there stood a famous and beautiful city named Kanakpur. Its king was Dhandatt — a man of right faith, virtuous, and devoted to dharma. His minister was Shrivandak, a follower of Buddhism. Yet the king governed well with his minister's help and faced no obstacles.

One day, as the king and minister sat in the palace discussing affairs of state, the king beheld two monks travelling through the sky, endowed with supernatural powers. Overjoyed, the king rose and humbly saluted them, inviting them into his palace. Truly it is said: "The company of saints is dear to the good."

At the king's request, the monks gave religious discourse, and upon departing, they took Minister Shrivandak with them. They instructed him, and when he expressed a desire for spiritual welfare, they bestowed upon him the vows of a layman. Shrivandak returned home. Previously, he had visited his Buddhist teacher daily to pay respects. But after taking Jain vows, he ceased going. The Buddhist guru summoned him, and when Shrivandak came but did not bow, the guru Sanghshri asked why. Shrivandak explained everything — the monks' arrival, their teaching, and his acceptance of vows.

Hearing this, Sanghshri spoke with great sorrow: "Alas! You have been deceived! The wicked have played a great trick on you. Is it possible for anyone to walk in the unsupported sky? Your king must be a great deceiver and illusionist. That is why he showed you this marvel and drew you into his religion. You were so devoted to the Buddha, yet you fell for that wicked king's tricks!" He went on: "From now on, never go to the royal court, and if you must, never tell the king of today's events. He is a Jain and will naturally have no love for Buddhism."

But Shrivandak was a man of discernment. He had tasted the truth of the Jain dharma and could not be swayed by false arguments. He replied calmly: "Gurudev, what you say is not right. The monks I saw were genuine saints of great austerity, and their teachings illuminated my soul. I cannot abandon the path of truth for mere words of doubt."

The minister's steadfast faith could not be shaken. He continued in his Jain vows and ultimately attained great spiritual progress. The story teaches that true faith, once properly established through genuine experience, cannot be destroyed by the cunning arguments of those who wish to mislead. Discernment and direct experience of truth are stronger than any deception.
